latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Antecedent infection, vaccination, or undefined environmental trigger priming innate immune cells in genetically susceptible host; often subclinical or as nonspecific viral prodrome 1-4 weeks before AOSD onset.

Composite innate-immune autoinflammatory storm characteristic of AOSD; integrates IL-1/IL-18, IL-6 and IFN-γ axes plus neutrophil/macrophage activation; correlates with quotidian fever, evanescent rash, hyperferritinemia.
Core pathogenic axis of AOSD; massive IL-18 elevation (often disproportionate to IL-1β) drives fever, neutrophilia, NK dysfunction and predisposes to MAS; targeted by anakinra/canakinumab.

Drives hepatic acute-phase response: CRP, fibrinogen, ferritin, ESR, hepcidin-mediated anemia of inflammation, thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminemia; correlates with arthritis chronicity; targeted by tocilizumab.
Activated lymphocyte/macrophage IFN-γ signaling that becomes dominant when AOSD transitions to MAS; reflected in serum CXCL9 and sCD25.
Granulocyte-skewed myelopoiesis with left shift, immature neutrophils, NETosis; underlies marked leukocytosis (often 15-30 ×10^9/L) with ≥80% PMN that is part of Yamaguchi criteria.

Cytokine-driven hepatic Kupffer-cell activation and lymphoreticular infiltration causing transaminitis, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy and ferritin hypersecretion with low glycosylation fraction.

Pre-clinical drift toward MAS: rising ferritin trajectory, falling platelets/fibrinogen/ESR paradox, rising LDH/triglycerides, while overt HLH criteria not yet met; observed in ~30-40% of active AOSD and overtly progresses in ~15%.

Hyperactivated tissue macrophages with hemophagocytosis; clinically: very high ferritin (>10,000), splenomegaly, cytopenias, hypofibrinogenemia, hypertriglyceridemia, transaminitis, sCD25 elevation, low NK cytotoxicity. Major driver of mortality in AOSD.
Macrophage-driven consumptive coagulopathy with hypofibrinogenemia, prolonged PT/aPTT, elevated D-dimer, and hemorrhagic risk during active MAS.
Persistent cytokine exposure causing organ injury (hepatitis, myocarditis, ARDS, reactive amyloid risk in chronic disease); proportional to disease activity × time without adequate suppression.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Pathogen/PAMP/DAMP exposure activates NLRP3 inflammasome in innate immune cells of genetically susceptible host, releasing mature IL-1β and IL-18.
IL-1/IL-18 are upstream pivots of the AOSD cytokine storm; suppression by anakinra usually collapses the entire phenotype within days, demonstrating causal centrality.
IL-1β is a canonical inducer of hepatocyte and stromal IL-6 production, driving the acute-phase response.
IL-1 and IL-18 promote G-CSF release and neutrophil mobilization/maturation arrest, producing leukocytosis with left shift.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: particularly when IL-18 dominant and/or NK cytotoxicity reduced
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: IL-18 strongly synergizes with IL-12 to drive Th1/NK IFN-γ secretion; this transition signals shift toward MAS.
Hepatocyte CRP synthesis is essentially IL-6 dependent; CRP often >100 mg/L during flares.
Fibrinogen and other acute-phase proteins increase RBC rouleaux formation and ESR; tocilizumab characteristically normalizes ESR rapidly.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: fibrinogen is high in active AOSD without MAS but falls in MAS due to consumption
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: IL-6 drives hepatic fibrinogen synthesis; absolute level may still be 'normal' in MAS despite consumption (relative hypofibrinogenemia).
Negative acute-phase reactant; chronic IL-6 signaling and capillary leak reduce serum albumin.
Hepcidin-mediated iron sequestration and erythropoiesis suppression cause anemia of chronic inflammation.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: applies in active AOSD without MAS; reverses if MAS develops
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: IL-6 stimulates thrombopoietin; reactive thrombocytosis (often 400-800 ×10^9/L) typical of AOSD without MAS.
IL-1, IL-6, TNF and IL-18 act on hypothalamic POA producing characteristic quotidian fever ≥39°C with afebrile interval, typically late afternoon/evening.
Salmon-pink macular/maculopapular rash on trunk/proximal limbs co-localizes with fever spikes via cytokine-induced cutaneous neutrophil infiltrates; resolves between spikes.
Symmetric polyarthritis (knees, wrists, ankles) is a Yamaguchi major criterion; in chronic articular subset persists after systemic features resolve.
Non-suppurative pharyngitis (cricothyroiditis) is a near-pathognomonic minor criterion present in 50-70% of patients.
Diffuse myalgia synchronous with fever spikes is common; rarely with elevated CK.
Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia driven by IL-6/TNF; cervical and generalized adenopathy in 50-65%.
Hepatic Kupffer-cell activation and lymphocytic infiltration produce palpable hepatomegaly in 30-50%.
Reticuloendothelial activation produces splenomegaly in 40-55%; more severe in MAS.
Mild-moderate transaminitis in 50-75%; severe rises (>1000 U/L) suggest fulminant hepatitis or MAS.
Parallels ALT in AOSD hepatic involvement.
Elevated LDH reflects hepatic, hematologic and tissue turnover; markedly elevated in MAS.
Activated hepatocytes and macrophages secrete enormous quantities of ferritin; values 5-50× upper normal are characteristic and >10,000 ng/mL strongly raises suspicion for MAS.
In AOSD glycosylation machinery is saturated; glycosylated fraction <20% (vs normal 50-80%); combination of high ferritin and low glycosylated fraction is highly specific.
Leukocytosis ≥10 ×10^9/L (often 15-30) with ≥80% PMN is a Yamaguchi major criterion.
Granulocyte-skewed myelopoiesis; ANC frequently >10 ×10^9/L during flare.
Left shift with band forms reflects intense myeloid demand; can mimic bacterial infection.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: stronger when IL-18 disproportionately elevated and/or NK cytotoxicity impaired
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Sustained IL-18 with NK dysfunction reduces cytotoxic clearance of activated antigen-presenting cells, building pressure toward overt MAS.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: transition probability ~10-20% in active AOSD; higher with EBV/CMV reactivation, infection, or DMARD initiation
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: When macrophage activation pressure crosses a threshold, frank MAS develops with hemophagocytosis and multi-organ involvement.
MAS is dominated by IFN-γ signaling; serum CXCL9 and sCD25 sharply rise.
Hemophagocytosis and consumptive coagulopathy reduce platelet count; falling platelets in AOSD with rising ferritin is an early MAS warning.
Macrophage erythrophagocytosis and marrow suppression; cytopenias are an HLH-2004 criterion.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: MAS may paradoxically lower ANC even though baseline AOSD raises it; the inflection is diagnostically informative
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Marrow phagocytosis reduces neutrophils; falling ANC during a presumed AOSD flare should prompt MAS evaluation.
MAS produces extreme hyperferritinemia, frequently >10,000-50,000 ng/mL; a sharp upward inflection signals decompensation.
TNF/IFN-γ inhibit lipoprotein lipase; hypertriglyceridemia is HLH-2004 criterion.
Activated T-cells shed sIL-2R; sCD25 ≥2400 U/mL is HLH-2004 criterion and tracks MAS activity.
CXCL9 is an IFN-γ-induced chemokine; among most sensitive biomarkers for MAS in AOSD.
Reduced NK cytotoxicity is HLH-2004 criterion and a mechanistic driver, not just a biomarker.
Marrow biopsy showing histiocytes engulfing blood cells; absence does not exclude MAS.
Macrophage hyperactivation drives consumptive coagulopathy via tissue factor and plasminogen activator release.
Falling/normal-range fibrinogen during severe inflammation (where it should be high) is an HLH-2004 criterion.
Activation of coagulation/fibrinolysis raises D-dimer to high levels.
Consumption of clotting factors and hepatic impairment prolong PT/INR.
Severe MAS-associated coagulopathy progresses to overt DIC with hemorrhagic risk.
AOSD-MAS can progress to fulminant hepatic failure with markedly elevated transaminases, jaundice, and coagulopathy; major mortality contributor.
Cytokine-driven alveolar capillary injury can produce ARDS, especially in MAS.
Cytokine-mediated cardiac inflammation; myocarditis or pericarditis with tamponade described in severe AOSD.
Pericarditis/pleuritis present in 20-40%; usually small effusions but tamponade rare.
MAS itself drives the MAS event hazard; this is the proximate mechanism.
MAS is the leading cause of AOSD mortality; case-fatality 10-25% in MAS, vs <5% in AOSD without MAS.
Acute liver failure carries high short-term mortality.
ARDS in cytokine storm carries substantial ICU mortality.
Overt DIC adds hemorrhagic and thrombotic mortality.
Prolonged uncontrolled disease accumulates organ injury and predisposes to MAS, secondary infection from prolonged steroids, and chronic articular destruction.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: represents low prior, not active suppression
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Negative ANA (<1:80) is a Yamaguchi minor criterion; AOSD is autoinflammatory not autoimmune so adaptive autoantibodies are characteristically absent.
Negative RF is a Yamaguchi minor criterion; positivity should prompt reconsideration of seropositive RA or other connective tissue disease.
Direct biomarker of one of the major drivers; useful when tocilizumab response monitored.
Surrogate of IL-1/IL-18 activity (where measurable); IL-18 itself often grossly elevated and disease-specific.
Sinus tachycardia accompanies fever spikes and inflammatory state.
The disease can present with persistent or recurrent fever over the observed clinical history.
AOSD often presents as antibiotic-refractory fever because the driver is sterile autoinflammation.

axes.shape_free_text: Quotidian / double-quotidian spiking pattern: 1-2 daily peaks ≥39°C, often late afternoon-evening, returning to or below normal between spikes; pattern resolves rapidly with effective treatment.
Salmon-pink macular/maculopapular rash on trunk and proximal limbs, often Koebner-positive; appears with fever spikes and fades when afebrile.
Symmetric polyarthritis/arthralgia (knees, wrists, ankles, MCP/PIP); systemic-predominant subset has transient arthritis, chronic articular subset has persistent destructive arthritis.
Non-suppurative pharyngitis often early prodrome; cricothyroid pain may be present.
Diffuse myalgia synchronous with fever spikes.
Cervical or generalized adenopathy in 50-65%; biopsy shows reactive paracortical hyperplasia, must distinguish from lymphoma.
Palpable in 40-55%; more pronounced in MAS.
Palpable liver in 30-50%, with transaminitis.
Pleuritis or pericarditis with mostly small effusions; tamponade rare.
Marked leukocytosis ≥10 (often 15-30); may fall below 10 if MAS develops.
≥80% of WBC; typically 8-25 ×10^9/L; falls in MAS.
Left shift with bands and metamyelocytes; can confound bacterial infection workup.
Reactive thrombocytosis (400-800) in active AOSD without MAS; sharp drop into normal/low range with rising ferritin signals MAS.
axes.second_peak: In MAS the trajectory inverts: platelets fall to <100 ×10^9/L within days, often the earliest cytopenia.

axes.shape_free_text: Mild-moderate normocytic anemia of inflammation; sharp drop in MAS.
Hallmark: typically 1,000-10,000 in active AOSD; >5x ULN in 70%, >10,000 raises high concern for MAS or hyperferritinemic syndrome; rapid response to effective therapy.
Markedly reduced in AOSD; <0.20 with high total ferritin has high specificity (>80%) for AOSD vs other hyperferritinemic states.
Markedly elevated, often >100 mg/L; tracks IL-6 axis.
Markedly elevated; falls slowly; in MAS may paradoxically drop because of fibrinogen consumption.
Mild-moderate transaminitis in 50-75%; severe rises (>1000) suggest fulminant AOSD hepatitis or MAS, sometimes also DMARD/NSAID hepatotoxicity.
Parallels ALT; ratio AST>ALT may emerge in MAS or alcohol/drug overlap.
Elevated reflecting tissue/hematologic turnover; very high in MAS.
Reduced as negative acute-phase reactant; recovery follows IL-6 suppression.
Elevated as acute-phase reactant in active AOSD; falls in MAS to <250 or even <150 mg/dL despite ongoing inflammation (paradox).
axes.second_peak: In MAS fibrinogen drops sharply to 100-300 mg/dL within days.

axes.shape_free_text: Often normal in pure AOSD; rises in MAS to >265 mg/dL (HLH-2004 criterion).
Elevated in active AOSD, very high in MAS (≥2400 U/mL HLH-2004 criterion); ratio sCD25/ferritin sometimes used to distinguish AOSD-MAS from primary HLH.
IFN-γ-inducible chemokine; rises sharply in MAS; emerging biomarker.
Markedly elevated; correlates with CRP and arthritis; tocilizumab raises measured IL-6 by blocking receptor binding (interpret with caution after Toci).
IL-1β often modestly elevated; IL-18 (closely related, often measured separately) can be 10-1000× normal in AOSD.
Negative or low-titer; positive ANA should prompt reconsideration of SLE/connective tissue disease.
Negative (Yamaguchi minor criterion).
Histiocytes engulfing blood cells in marrow biopsy; supportive of MAS but absence does not exclude.
Decreased in MAS; HLH-2004 criterion when low or absent.
Elevated in active inflammation; very high in MAS-DIC.
Usually normal in pure AOSD; prolonged in fulminant hepatitis or MAS-DIC.
Often only mildly elevated despite high CRP/ferritin in pure AOSD; helps distinguish from bacterial sepsis but is not specific.
Sinus tachycardia accompanies fever spikes; persistent tachycardia out of proportion may suggest myocarditis/pericarditis.
Subacute weight loss common during prolonged active disease.
Daily probability of overt MAS; ~10-15% lifetime cumulative; elevated during flares, infection triggers, or DMARD initiation.
Rare but feared; usually in MAS context or on hepatotoxic agents (NSAIDs, MTX); higher in early diagnosis.
Mostly arises in MAS; otherwise rare.
Cytokine-storm related; uncommon but reported, mostly in severe MAS.
Rare (<5%); cytokine-mediated; pericarditis with tamponade reported.
Rises with high-dose steroids, biologic therapy, neutropenia from MAS or cytotoxics.
Overall AOSD case-fatality ~5%; rises substantially with MAS (10-25%), fulminant hepatitis, ARDS, and severe DIC; very low in well-controlled monocyclic disease.
Confidence that AOSD-MAS (vs. primary HLH or sepsis-driven HLH) is the active mechanism, governing whether HLH-94/etoposide pathway should be invoked vs. AOSD-targeted IL-1/IL-6/IFN-γ blockade.
Probability that an active infection (EBV, CMV, parvovirus, bacterial sepsis) is precipitating or mimicking the flare; modulates immunosuppression intensity.
Lymphoma can mimic AOSD; persistent atypical adenopathy, B-symptoms, failure to respond, age >60 should trigger biopsy.
Higher in older patients, persistent isolated lymphadenopathy, weight loss, atypical course.
Reactivation of TB/HBV with biologic therapy; screening required before initiation.
Composite susceptibility to opportunistic and bacterial infection on chronic immunosuppression.
Modifies eligibility for MTX, NSAIDs, and risks of hepatotoxic biologics.
Active uncontrolled infection contraindicates initiation/escalation of biologic immunosuppression.
Modulates choice between MTX (contraindicated), anakinra (data reassuring), tocilizumab, low-dose steroids.
History-level fever burden over days to months, distinct from a single measured body temperature.

axes.display_name: Lack of clinical response to standard antibacterial therapy
axes.shape_free_text: Persistent fever, inflammation, or organ findings despite antibacterial therapy that should have covered ordinary bacterial infection.

axis_couplings.conditionality: applies once subclinical_macrophage_activation_pressure begins to rise; opposite sign in early uncomplicated AOSD where both rise together
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Sharp ferritin rise with falling platelets is a near-pathognomonic MAS warning; this drift arises from the macrophage activation pressure, not from independent noise.

axis_couplings.conditionality: MAS-onset behavior; in uncomplicated AOSD both rise together
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Falling fibrinogen during severe inflammation is the consumption signature of MAS-DIC.
Rash characteristically appears with fever spikes and fades when afebrile; this synchrony is itself a diagnostic clue.

axis_couplings.conditionality: decouples and inverts in MAS where ESR can paradoxically fall as fibrinogen consumes
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: ESR is largely fibrinogen-driven; the paradoxical ESR drop with high CRP is a MAS clue.
Hepatic injury moves both transaminases together; isolated AST elevation suggests muscle/hemolysis or alcohol contribution.

axis_couplings.conditionality: after tocilizumab, CRP is suppressed while measured IL-6 rises; coupling inverts
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Hepatic CRP synthesis is essentially IL-6 dependent; this is mechanistically coupled.
Subclinical drift crossing threshold defines transition to overt MAS; the threshold is fuzzy and individualized.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: NSAIDs aggravate AOSD-related transaminitis and rarely fulminant hepatitis.

failure_modes: Monotherapy fails to control disease in >75% of AOSD
May obscure fever pattern and delay correct diagnosis
treatments.context_specific_role: Diagnostic bridging while ruling out infection/malignancy and during work-up; symptom relief only.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Initiate only after blood cultures drawn and infection mimic reasonably excluded; otherwise progresses sepsis.
High-dose pulse steroids (methylprednisolone 1g × 3) are first-line for AOSD-MAS.

failure_modes: Steroid dependence (cannot taper below 7.5-10 mg without flare) common
Many adverse effects on long-term use
treatments.context_specific_role: Mainstay induction (0.5-1 mg/kg/day prednisolone); pulse 500-1000 mg methylprednisolone × 3 days for severe systemic disease or AOSD-MAS; tapered over months once steroid-sparing agent in place.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Hepatotoxicity can be confused with AOSD hepatitis; avoid in active transaminitis.
Teratogenic; women must use contraception, men should also pause before conception.

failure_modes: Slow onset (6-12 weeks) inadequate for severe systemic flares
Stronger effect on chronic articular than systemic features
treatments.context_specific_role: Steroid-sparing agent for chronic articular AOSD or steroid-dependent systemic disease; combine with folate.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Anakinra is increasingly first-line in AOSD-MAS owing to short half-life, safety in infection, and mechanistic targeting of IL-1/IL-18 axis; high doses (4-10 mg/kg/day) used in severe cases.
Among biologics, anakinra has the most favorable infection profile and is typically preferred when infection cannot be fully excluded.

failure_modes: Some chronic articular cases respond less well than systemic

side_effects.interpretation: factor multiplier; rare DRESS-like reaction reported

treatments.context_specific_role: Highly effective in systemic AOSD; standard 100 mg SC daily, escalate up to 4-10 mg/kg/day in MAS; rapid response (24-72 h) and short half-life make it ideal when infection or MAS is suspected.

failure_modes: Long half-life is a liability if infection emerges
Some IL-18-dominant or IFN-γ-dominant phenotypes (notably MAS) respond less well than to anakinra
treatments.context_specific_role: Maintenance for established responders; q4-week SC dosing avoids daily injections of anakinra; AOSD/sJIA approved indication in many regions.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Particularly effective for chronic articular AOSD and steroid-resistant systemic disease.

failure_modes: Hepatotoxicity in some, can mimic AOSD flare
Rare association with paradoxical MAS triggering
GI perforation in patients with diverticulitis

side_effects.interpretation: factor multiplier; suppresses biomarker independent of underlying activity

treatments.context_specific_role: Strong option for systemic and articular AOSD, especially chronic-articular subset; 8 mg/kg IV q2-4 weeks or SC weekly; caution if AOSD-MAS suspected (long half-life, may mask, occasional reports of triggering MAS).

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Suppresses T-cell IFN-γ production and is a recognized salvage component in AOSD-MAS.

treatments.context_specific_role: Salvage therapy in AOSD-MAS or refractory cytopenia; effective T-cell suppressant; declining use as IL-1/IL-6 biologics dominate.
Adjunct in severe disease especially when infection cannot be excluded or in pregnancy; not standard of care.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Etoposide-based HLH-94 protocol is reserved for severe steroid-refractory MAS/HLH; effective at depleting activated cytotoxic T cells and macrophages.

treatments.context_specific_role: Reserved for refractory AOSD-MAS not controlled by pulse steroids + anakinra ± cyclosporine; dose-reduced from primary HLH protocols.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: IFN-γ blockade is rational in MAS where IFN-γ axis dominates; emerging evidence in refractory AOSD-MAS.

treatments.context_specific_role: Targeted IFN-γ blockade for refractory MAS, currently more established in primary HLH; off-label/expanded access in AOSD-MAS.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Etanercept/infliximab/adalimumab have modest effect on chronic articular AOSD; less effective for systemic features.

failure_modes: Limited efficacy on systemic features compared with IL-1/IL-6 blockade
treatments.context_specific_role: Third-line option for chronic articular AOSD if IL-1/IL-6 blockade unavailable or contraindicated.

young_adult_16_to_35.trajectory_modulation: Classic peak incidence; systemic-predominant phenotype more common.

middle_aged_36_to_60.trajectory_modulation: Second smaller incidence peak; more chronic articular phenotype.

older_than_60.trajectory_modulation: Atypical; lymphoma must be excluded; higher MAS and mortality risk when AOSD does occur.

female.trajectory_modulation: Slight female predominance; pregnancy planning may modify therapy choice.

hla_drb1_susceptibility_allele.trajectory_modulation: HLA-DRB1*15, DRB1*14 and others have been associated; phenotype subtyping (systemic vs chronic articular) also has HLA correlates.

recent_viral_infection_within_4_weeks.trajectory_modulation: EBV, parvovirus B19, CMV, rubella, coxsackie, influenza, SARS-CoV-2 reported as triggers; symptom onset typically 1-4 weeks post-trigger.

east_asian.trajectory_modulation: AOSD reported with relatively high prevalence in Japan, Korea, China; MAS rates also reported high in East Asian cohorts.

prior_sjia.trajectory_modulation: Adult-onset Still's disease is now considered the same disease as sJIA on the autoinflammatory IL-1/IL-18 spectrum; recurrence in adulthood plausible.

supportive_care: Yamaguchi (or Fautrel) criteria-based diagnosis only after exhaustive exclusion of infection (blood/urine cultures, EBV/CMV/parvovirus B19 PCR, HIV, hepatitis serologies, TB screen), malignancy (especially lymphoma — low threshold for lymph node biopsy, peripheral smear review, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis), and other rheumatic mimics (SLE, vasculitis, RA)

Daily monitoring during induction: temperature curve, complete blood count with differential, CRP, ferritin, fibrinogen, AST/ALT, LDH, triglycerides, creatinine — paying close attention to ferritin trajectory and platelet/fibrinogen drops as MAS warning signs

Active surveillance for MAS: low threshold to apply Ravelli/2016 EULAR-PRINTO MAS criteria when ferritin rising rapidly, platelets or fibrinogen falling, transaminases rising, or new cytopenia; consider bone marrow exam, sCD25, CXCL9, NK function in unclear cases

Pre-biologic screening: tuberculosis (IGRA + chest imaging), HBV (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs), HCV, HIV, varicella history; vaccinate with inactivated vaccines (pneumococcal, influenza, hepatitis B, COVID-19, shingles) before immunosuppression where possible; avoid live vaccines while on biologics
Bone protection: vitamin D and calcium repletion, DXA at baseline, bisphosphonates for prolonged steroid courses (typically ≥7.5 mg prednisolone for >3 months)
Glucose, blood pressure, lipid monitoring during steroid therapy; PJP prophylaxis (TMP-SMX) if on combined high-dose steroids and other immunosuppression
Reproductive counseling: methotrexate contraindicated in pregnancy; anakinra has reassuring safety data in pregnancy; coordinate with obstetrics if pregnant or planning pregnancy
Ophthalmology referral if features overlap with sJIA (uveitis screening) or on long-term steroids (cataract, glaucoma)
Physical and occupational therapy for chronic articular AOSD; joint protection and range-of-motion exercises to prevent destructive ankylosis (especially carpal/tarsal)
Psychosocial support: chronic remitting illness in young adults often impacts education, employment, fertility, and mental health; access to social work and patient organizations

If MAS diagnosed: ICU-level monitoring with close attention to coagulopathy, hepatic synthetic function, hemodynamics, oxygenation; transfusion support per parameters; rapid escalation pathway (high-dose steroids → high-dose anakinra → cyclosporine/etoposide/emapalumab); evaluate for and treat any infectious trigger in parallel

Long-term follow-up: assess for AA amyloidosis (proteinuria, renal function) in long-standing uncontrolled disease; periodic re-evaluation of need for ongoing immunosuppression in monocyclic patients with sustained remission
